forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: East Hertfordshire secures audit rebuild plan after four years of disclaimed opinions
news_drafts.lead: East Hertfordshire's external auditors have set out a plan to rebuild assurance on the council's accounts following four consecutive years of disclaimed opinions, the most serious audit outcome. The build-back work, to be undertaken alongside the 2025/26 and 2026/27 audits, will cost £245,524 beyond the standard audit fee and is expected to create pressure on the council's revenue budget across 2026/27 and 2027/28. The auditors have named capacity constraints in both their team and the council's finance team as the main risk to completing the work and delivering an opinion by the statutory deadline of 31 January 2027. Separately, the council's 2026/27 revenue outturn shows a £440k overspend, primarily driven by Place services, which overspent by £338k, and a shortfall of £404k in planned income from Regeneration, Customer and Commercial Services.

news_drafts.headline: East Hertfordshire in audit rebuild after four years of disclaimed opinions
news_drafts.lead: East Hertfordshire received disclaimed audit opinions for four consecutive years from 2021/22 to 2024/25, the most serious audit outcome. The council and its auditors have now mapped a structured rebuild plan to restore assurance on the council's accounts, but face capacity constraints in delivering it. The additional audit work will cost £245,524 beyond the standard fee and create pressure on the revenue budget across 2026/27 and 2027/28. Both the council's finance team and the audit team have identified capacity as the main risk to completing the rebuild and delivering an audit opinion by the 31 January 2027 statutory deadline. The council also recorded a net service overspend of £440k in 2026/27 and delayed £237k of capital projects including URC Church Hall and town centre regeneration work into 2027/28.

news_drafts.headline: East Hertfordshire faces four years of failed audits and £440k revenue overspend as rebuild plan delays capital projects
news_drafts.lead: East Hertfordshire received disclaimed audit opinions — the most serious audit outcome, where auditors cannot form an opinion on whether the council's accounts are fairly presented — for the fourth consecutive year in 2024/25. The council's auditors have committed to a "build-back plan" to restore assurance on the accounts, but the work will cost an additional £245,524 beyond the standard £185,917 audit fee, creating acknowledged pressure on the revenue budget across 2026/27 and 2027/28. The council's operational position adds to the strain: net cost of services overspent by £440k in 2026/27, with Place service accounting for £338k of that and Regeneration, Customer and Commercial Services failing to deliver £404k of planned income. Capacity constraints in both the audit team and the council's own finance function are identified as the primary risk to completing the rebuild work and delivering an audit opinion by the 31 January 2027 statutory deadline. Two capital projects — URC Church Hall and Old River Lane town centre regeneration — have been carried forward from 2026/27 to 2027/28, deferring £237k of planned spending.

findings.headline: General Fund balances assessed as adequate but earmarked reserves under review to identify resources for redeployment to support medium-term sustainability
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer has determined that General Fund balances remain adequate to support financial resilience, with a minimum level calculated at £3.578 million for 2027/28 based on risk factors including service demand volatility, inflationary pressures, commercial income uncertainty and Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty. However, the council is undertaking a comprehensive review of earmarked reserves to ensure they remain appropriately aligned to strategic priorities and financial risks, and to identify whether resources can be released to support medium-term financial sustainability. The outcome will be reported as part of the draft budget in January 2027.
findings.matters: Whilst balances are currently adequate, the potential release of earmarked reserves suggests the council may need to redeploy funds to address the medium-term budget gap, indicating tightening financial headroom.
findings.figures: Minimum General Fund balance: £3.578 million for 2027/28; Gross Revenue Expenditure 3% = £2.927m, Annual Gross Capital Expenditure 4% = £0.085m, Council Tax adjustment 4% = £0.566m
findings.quote: A review of earmarked reserves is currently being undertaken to ensure that reserves remain appropriately aligned to the Council's strategic priorities, financial risks and emerging commitments, including preparations for Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Council holds approximately £50 million borrowing with 4.5% annual cost assumptions throughout planning period
findings.detail: The MTFP notes that the council has approximately £50 million of borrowing outstanding. The financial plan assumes borrowing costs of 4.5% annually, based on current Public Works Loan Board rates and market forecasts, described as prudent assumptions. Given the scale of the borrowing, changes in interest rates could have a significant material impact on the council's financing costs and overall financial position.
findings.matters: A substantial borrowing book means interest rate movements could materially improve or worsen the financial position; if rates fall, the position improves, but they are assumed to remain elevated at 4.5%.
findings.figures: Council borrowing: approximately £50 million; assumed borrowing interest rate: 4.5% throughout planning period
findings.quote: With approximately £50 million of borrowing, changes in Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) and wider market interest rates can have a significant impact on financing costs and the Council's overall financial position.

findings.headline: 2027/28 savings programme of £623,000 identified; only £130,000 of further savings proposed for 2028/29, leaving later years without defined solutions
findings.detail: The council has identified £623,000 of recurring savings for 2027/28, comprising civil parking enforcement (£273,000), transformation team restructure (£255,000), ground maintenance re-procurement (£50,000), garden waste charges (£30,000), and EV charger income (£15,000). For 2028/29, only £130,000 of savings are currently identified. The council has also deferred £100,000 of previously anticipated car parking income from 2027/28 to 2028/29, reflecting uncertainty about achievable income levels from tariff reviews.
findings.matters: The concentration of identified savings in year one, with minimal savings identified for subsequent years, indicates that most of the remaining gap (years 2-5 totalling £1.398 million cumulative) currently lacks defined solutions.
findings.figures: 2027/28 recurring savings £623,000 (civil parking £273k, transformation £255k, maintenance £50k, waste £30k, EV £15k); 2028/29 savings £130,000; car parking income reprofiled: £100,000 deferred
findings.quote: The current MTFP includes £623k of recurring savings in 2027/28, reducing the remaining savings requirement for that year to £283k

findings.headline: Council retains £818,000 annual provision for Local Government Reorganisation costs despite government pause on the programme
findings.detail: Although the government announced on 7 September 2026 that it was pausing Local Government Reorganisation implementation activity pending a review of the national programme, East Hertfordshire has retained financial provisions totalling £818,000 annually (£500,000 for implementation and transition costs, £318,000 for potential workforce transition and redundancy costs) in both 2026/27 and 2027/28. The council considers these provisions prudent given the uncertainty around the outcome and timetable of the government review.
findings.matters: The council is maintaining material contingency provisions for an uncertain event; if reorganisation is significantly delayed or abandoned, these could be released; if accelerated, they may prove insufficient.
findings.figures: LGR provision 2027/28: £500,000 implementation costs plus £318,000 workforce transition/redundancy reserve; total £818,000 annually
findings.quote: Provision of £0.5 million in both 2026/27 and 2027/28 has been included to support potential transition and implementation costs should reorganisation proceed in the future. In addition, the Council has earmarked £318,000 in both years to support potential workforce transition and redundancy costs.

findings.headline: BEAM Theatre venue revised to break-even target, creating £375,000 additional budget pressure
findings.detail: Following a comprehensive review of the council's theatre venue's operating model and financial performance during 2026, the MTFP now assumes a break-even position from 2027/28 onwards, rather than the surplus previously forecast. The council acknowledges that the venue requires time to build audience levels and sustainable income streams, and that previous surplus assumptions were unachievable. This represents a permanent £375,000 pressure on the council's budget.
findings.matters: A commercial venue unable to deliver previously forecast surpluses demonstrates challenges in generating discretionary income and signals the need to offset this through other budget measures.
findings.figures: Budget pressure from BEAM Theatre: £375,000 in 2027/28
findings.quote: The revised business plan identified that the surplus assumptions included within the MTFP were unlikely to be achieved in the medium term. The MTFP has therefore been updated to assume a break-even position from 2027/28 onwards.
